planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Lemon Gold is a California-origin selection noted for cycling through several light bloom flushes across the year rather than setting one heavy crop, which spreads out the harvest window and lets fruit be picked a bit early and still finish ripening well off the tree.

directions: Site Lemon Gold in full sun with well-drained, fertile soil and shelter from strong wind, since it is somewhat less vigorous than other white sapote selections and benefits from a protected spot. The tree tends toward repeated light bloom cycles rather than one big flush, so ripe fruit can be found across a longer window, with the main crop typically coming on in fall. Fruit is medium-to-large, thin-skinned, and turns yellow as it ripens, with smooth flesh carrying a sweet, custardy flavor that growers often describe as having a faint lemony or citrus note setting it apart from other white sapote cultivars. Because it holds flavor well even when picked slightly under-ripe and finished indoors, Lemon Gold is a forgiving choice for growers who want to beat fruit fly or bird pressure.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; McDill is a precocious Orange County, California selection that can begin bearing sooner than many other white sapote cultivars and grafts readily onto seedling rootstock, ripening its crop in early autumn.

directions: Plant McDill in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil sheltered from strong wind; it is a large, vigorous tree that grows quickly and takes readily to grafting, making it a popular choice for growers wanting a dependable, early-bearing selection. Fruit is oblate in shape, greenish-yellow at maturity, and counts among the largest-fruited white sapote cultivars, with rich, custard-like flesh and excellent flavor. The crop ripens in early autumn, somewhat ahead of many other cultivars, giving Gulf Coast growers a jump on the harvest season before cooler weather sets in. Because the tree bears at a young age relative to seedling trees, it is a good option for growers wanting a quicker return from a newly planted grafted specimen.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Subtropical Fruit Trees for South Texas

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Reinecke Commercial is a San Diego-origin selection bred with shipping in mind, and its comparatively firm, longer-holding fruit makes it more forgiving of a short delay between harvest and eating than many softer-fleshed white sapote cultivars.

directions: Grow Reinecke Commercial in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil away from strong wind, as with other white sapote selections. As the cultivar name suggests, it was selected with commercial handling in mind: the fruit is somewhat irregular in shape, runs around five ounces, and turns a distinctive golden-orange as it ripens. Its standout trait among white sapote cultivars is better-than-average keeping quality, since many white sapote selections soften and spoil quickly after harvest, making Reinecke Commercial a useful choice for growers who want a few extra days of shelf life before the fruit must be eaten. Harvest when the skin has colored fully and the fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure, then hold at room temperature to finish ripening.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Wilson is one of the older named white sapote selections, valued for a reliably productive tree and good-flavored fruit, though it holds only briefly after harvest so plan to eat or process the crop promptly.

directions: Plant Wilson in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil sheltered from strong wind; it is a dependably heavy-bearing tree, one of the earlier California white sapote selections still grown today. The fruit is somewhat flattened rather than round, with good, rich, custardy flavor typical of the species, but it softens and turns quickly once picked and does not hold in storage as well as newer cultivars like Reinecke Commercial. For that reason, Wilson suits growers who plan to eat, share, or process fruit soon after harvest rather than store or ship it. Pick as soon as the fruit softens slightly at the stem end and use within a few days for best quality.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes

planting.note: Plant a grafted or container tree in spring in full sun on moist, well-drained, fertile soil in zone 9-11; Mac's Golden is a named selection of the woolly-leaf white sapote (Casimiroa tetrameria), distinguished from ordinary seedling trees by its large, aromatic, elongated fruit with relatively few seeds.

directions: Grow Mac's Golden in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, mulching the root zone and providing winter protection in the cooler parts of zone 9 as with other woolly-leaf white sapote trees. This Carlsbad, California-origin selection is prized among Casimiroa tetrameria seedlings for producing notably large, elongated-oval, golden-yellow fruit with a distinctive rich aroma and fewer seeds than typical, giving a higher proportion of edible custardy flesh per fruit. The flavor is sweet and buttery, similar to common white sapote but often considered richer by growers who have tasted both. Because it is a grafted selection rather than an unnamed seedling, it offers more predictable fruit quality and size than growing Casimiroa tetrameria from seed.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
Morton, J. — Fruits of Warm Climates (1987)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Louise is a Chula Vista, California selection noted for an unusually long harvest season, cropping intermittently from January into September rather than concentrating fruit into a single flush, which makes it a favorite recommendation for home gardens.

directions: Plant Louise in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil protected from strong wind. Its main appeal is an extended, nearly everbearing cropping pattern that stretches from midwinter through late summer instead of dumping the whole harvest at once, so a single home tree can supply ripe fruit across many months of the year. The medium-sized fruit ripens to yellow with the typical smooth, custard-textured white sapote flesh and good sweet flavor. Because of this spread-out bearing habit and generally manageable size, Louise is frequently recommended over larger, heavier-cropping cultivars for gardeners who want a steady trickle of fruit rather than a single big harvest to process at once.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in full sun to light shade on moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in zone 9b-11; False Jaboticaba is a Central American Myrciaria relative of the true jaboticaba, more cold-sensitive than that species, so give it a warm, wind-sheltered spot and protect it from temperatures much below 40°F.

directions: Site False Jaboticaba in full sun to light shade in moist, well-drained, organically rich, slightly acidic soil, and keep it out of cold wind since it bruises easily in temperatures much below 40°F even though established plants can shrug off a brief light frost. Native to roadside thickets and forest edges in Costa Rica, Panama, and Venezuela, this slow-growing evergreen shrub or small tree carries glossy foliage year-round and produces small, dark purple to nearly black, plum-scented berries about an inch across, distinctly bigger and thicker-skinned than fruit of true jaboticaba (Myrciaria/Plinia cauliflora). The thin, juicy, sweet-tart pulp surrounding one or two large seeds tastes grape-like but can run resinous, and the tough skin and seeds are not eaten, so most growers treat it as a fresh snacking or juicing fruit rather than a dessert-quality selection. A single well-established plant can set a heavy crop of fruit clustered along the branches, and its compact, ornamental habit makes it workable in large containers as well as in the ground for collectors wanting jaboticaba-adjacent species beyond the more common cauliflorous types.
sources: Top Tropicals — Myrciaria vexator (False Jaboticaba) Plant Encyclopedia
Plants For A Future (PFAF) — Myrciaria vexator
